storm.summary_layperson: Dry, sunny evening with no storms anywhere near the area — nothing for the local sea-breeze or marine-layer effects to work on tonight.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Air-water gap is already down to 2.9°F — below the marine-layer threshold and briefly negative by 7 PM — so there's no protective buffer tonight, though with no storms around there's nothing for it to blunt anyway.
storm.detail_html:
High pressure holds firm over the region this evening — the NWS Area Forecast Discussion (issued 2:31 PM) calls the pattern mainly dry through the next seven days, with the only mentioned thunderstorm chance arriving late Wednesday night into Thursday evening, well outside tonight's window.

Instability is essentially nonexistent: CAPE reads 0 J/kg off the HRRR, and the AFD's own language calls potential instability "limited." KOKX radar shows no storm cells within 50 miles, and there are no active NWS watches, advisories, or warnings.

The local Sound-effect modifier isn't a factor tonight regardless — there's no storm for it to blunt — but for the record it isn't available either: air and water are only 2.9°F apart (77°F air vs 74.1°F Sound water), well under the 5°F threshold for a meaningful marine layer, and the trend shows that gap essentially gone by 7 PM and briefly negative (air cooler than water) into the evening.

Bottom line for Riverside: a clear, dry, unremarkable evening. Nothing on radar, nothing in the pipeline, and no local mechanism in play one way or the other because there's nothing for it to modify. The call would only change if an unexpected cell fired well ahead of the AFD's Wednesday-night timeline — worth a radar glance if skies unexpectedly darken, but not expected.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light NW-to-W gradient wind with no sea breeze in play — starts around 7 kt at 5 PM and fades toward near-calm by 9–10 PM. Best pressure will be mid-cove away from the shoreline lee; don't expect this one to build, and don't count on much racing breeze after sunset.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today is a gradient-only evening (not a sea-breeze day): the inland-vs-Sound temperature differential is just 2.9°F, well under the 5°F threshold needed to build a thermal, and the sea-breeze ensemble confirms it — 0% of coastal stations and 0% of inland stations are showing southerly flow. Whatever wind exists is straight synoptic gradient, currently averaging 8.8 kt across the well-sited airport anemometers (KHVN, KHPN).

The HRRR hourly output (only reliable out to 7 PM tonight — later hours had fetch gaps) shows that gradient steadily unwinding through the window: NW 7 kt at 5 PM, backing to NW 5 kt at 6 PM, then W 4 kt by 7 PM, right around sunset (7:16 PM). Past that, there's no fresh model guidance, so 8–10 PM is extrapolated from the trend — expect it to keep fading toward 2–3 kt and effectively directionless. This is a fading-gradient evening, not a thermal collapse, but the practical result for racers is the same: less and less usable breeze as the night goes on.

One flag worth surfacing: Riverside YC's own station is reading a very different picture right now — ENE 6 kt gusting 15, versus the regional ensemble's NNW/NW ~330° at higher speed. That's a big divergence, well past the usual 45° flag, and with direction agreement across the network at just 0.58, this smells like a local eddy or terrain-driven shelter effect right at the cove rather than a real boundary. Trust the ensemble/HRRR for the open-Sound picture, but don't be surprised if the cove itself feels lighter and from an odd angle compared to what the forecast table says.

With NW-to-W flow that's puffy and offshore-influenced (per the cove geography: N–NW is gusty and shifty off the land, W–WNW channels down the Sound with holes near the CT shore), and direction agreement already weak, don't expect clean pressure on either shore tonight. Favor the middle of the cove, away from the immediate lee of the shoreline trees and houses, and play the puffs as they come rather than committing to a side.

For fleet planning: 5–7 kt at the start of the window is a fine one-design sweet spot, but by 8–9 PM this drops into drifter territory (2–4 kt) — light-air specialists only, with a real chance of going fully variable. If you're racing early in the window you'll get a decent sail; anything scheduled for 9 PM or later should expect very little breeze to work with.
